question: For the lines $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}-\hat{k})+\lambda(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$ and $\vec{r}=(2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+\hat{k})+\mu(\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k})$, establish that the lines are distinct and parallel and hence determine the shortest distance between them.
explanation:
Required Condition
Both lines have the same direction vector $\vec{b}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$. Hence, the lines are parallel. The first line passes through the point with position vector $\vec{a_1}=(1,0,-1)$, while the second passes through the point with position vector $\vec{a_2}=(2,3,1)$. Since $\vec{a_2}-\vec{a_1}=(1,3,2)$ is not proportional to $(1,2,2)$, the two lines are distinct.

Applying the Shortest Distance Formula
For distinct parallel lines $\vec{r}=\vec{a_1}+\lambda\vec{b}$ and $\vec{r}=\vec{a_2}+\mu\vec{b}$, the shortest distance is
$$d=\frac{\left|\vec{b}\times(\vec{a_2}-\vec{a_1})\right|}{|\vec{b}|}$$
Here,
$$\vec{b}\times(\vec{a_2}-\vec{a_1})=\begin{vmatrix}\hat{i}&\hat{j}&\hat{k}\\1&2&2\\1&3&2\end{vmatrix}=-2\hat{i}+\hat{k}$$
Therefore,
$$\left|\vec{b}\times(\vec{a_2}-\vec{a_1})\right|=\sqrt{(-2)^2+0^2+1^2}=\sqrt{5}$$
Also,
$$|\vec{b}|=\sqrt{1^2+2^2+2^2}=3$$
Hence,
$$d=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$$

Final Result
The two lines are distinct and parallel, and their shortest distance is $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ units.

options.A: The lines are coincident; shortest distance $0$.
options.B: The lines are distinct and parallel; shortest distance $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$ units.
options.C: The lines are distinct and parallel; shortest distance $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ units.
options.D: The lines are skew; shortest distance $\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}$ units.
